loading.status_physics: Getting the Monte Carlo physics sorted

0.s: The electric field legging it out of a closed surface is set by the charge inside. More charge, stronger field making a run for it through the surface.

1.s: Magnetic field lines stick together like glue, no start, no end. That's why there's no such thing as a magnetic monopole: a north pole always comes as a package deal with a south.

2.s: The gravitational potential at a point is the sum of every nearby mass doing its bit. Each bit lends a hand, and the farther off it sits, the less it counts.

3.t: A Mighty Tall Bridge in France
3.s: Stress inside a material is a tensor, so its value depends on the axes you pick. This formula shifts the stress components into another coordinate system using the rotation matrix Q.

4.s: Temperature changes for two reasons: swept along by the flow (advection) and spread out through diffusion, plus any heat source. This equation rolls all three into one.

calc.title: Multivariable Calculator
calc.hint: LaTeX input gets converted automatically (like Desmos). Use a physical keyboard or the on-screen keypad below.

graph.title: 3D Graph
graph.show_grad: Show the gradient field (on the xy plane)
graph.hint_gdomain: Type f(z) using z, i, pi, e and sin/cos/exp/log/sqrt. Hue = arg f, brightness = |f|. Drag = pan, scroll = zoom.
graph.hint_gfractal: Mandelbrot, Julia (set c) and Newton (roots of z³-1). Drag = pan, scroll = zoom.
graph.hint_gsurf3d: Surface z=f(x,y) + tangent plane, gradient vector and projected level curves. Sliders move the tangent point.
graph.hint_gfrenet: 3D parametric curve with Frenet frame T/N/B at point t. Kappa and tau are numeric. Drag to orbit.
graph.hint_gtrans3d: 3Blue1Brown-style 3D linear transformation: cube, grid and basis vectors follow the matrix. Morph slider interpolates I → A.
graph.hint_gslope: Slope field y'=f(x,y). Click anywhere to draw an RK4 solution from that point. Drag = pan, scroll = zoom.
graph.hint_gdist: Distribution PDF/CDF with live parameters and highlighted P(a≤X≤b) area. Sliders change parameters instantly.
graph.hint_ggraphalgo: Random weighted graph. Pick an algorithm and watch animated steps (gold = visited, bright = path/MST). Nodes are draggable.
graph.hint_gfield: Charges are draggable; gold lines = equipotentials, arrows = E field direction. Arrow length ∝ field strength.
graph.hint_gpvcycle: P-V diagram of Carnot/Otto/Diesel cycles with animated state point. Efficiency is computed from the parameters.
graph.hint_gising: 2D Ising model via Metropolis. Lower T below Tc≈2.27 to watch domains merge (magnetization rises).
graph.hint_gminkowski: Minkowski diagram: light cone, moving-frame axes and calibration hyperbola. Drag events to see invariant s².
graph.hint_gfluid: 2D fluid simulation (Jos Stam). Drag to inject ink and velocity; the dye follows the velocity field.
graph.hint_ggeodesic: Geodesics in the Schwarzschild metric (rs=1). Photons with b<1.5 are captured; large b get deflected. Massive orbits can precess.
graph.hint_gray: Two thin lenses with parallel incoming rays. Thin-lens formula applied at each surface. Negative f = concave lens.
graph.note_gdomain: f(z) \text{ ar an bplána casta},\ \mathrm{hue} = \arg f,\ \mathrm{shade} = |f|
graph.note_gslope: y' = f(x,y)\ \text{— cliceáil pointe tosaigh don réiteach RK4}
graph.note_ggraphalgo: \text{tarraing nóid, roghnaigh algartam, féach ar beochan na gcéimeanna}

catalog.b: A rake of ready-made experiments. Each one fills in the surface, field and domain for you, then you can meddle away to your heart's content. ELI5: it's like the set menu in a chippy, pick one, then jazz it up however you like.

surface.b: The "lay of the land" the electric field blows across. ELI5: picture a bedsheet getting pulled up and down; f(x,y) is how high the sheet sits at any spot (x,y). Flat sheet means f = 0, a hill means f = exp(-x^2-y^2) and so on. The fancy name is a 2D manifold in 3D space, if you're showing off.

domain.b:
The patch of ground under the sheet where Monte Carlo "throws the dice" to drop sample points. Units are metres (SI), so the area dx·dy comes out straight in m².
ELI5: it's the bit of the map you've picked for the experiment; the bigger the patch, the more flux lands in it.

field.b:
The field is like a "wind" shoving a wee +1 C charge about. Units are N/C (newtons per coulomb), same thing as V/m.
ELI5: drop a 1 C charge somewhere and a 500 N/C field means it's getting pushed and pulled with 500 newtons, no bother to it.

fieldmode.b:
Uniform: same strength and direction everywhere, like a steady breeze, deadly for learning the basics of flux.
Point charge: the field spreads out radially from one charge, fading off as 1/r² (Coulomb's law).
Free-form: you write the field bits P, Q, R yourself as functions of x, y, z. Grand.

strength.b:
How "hard" the field blows, in newtons per coulomb.
ELI5: think of E₀ as how heavy the rain is. For scale: cloudy day ~100 N/C, around the gaff ~100–300 N/C, a thunderstorm can hit thousands. Harder field, more flux through the surface (Φ ∝ E).

direction.b: Which way the field arrows point (3D). ELI5: rain can fall straight on your head (+z), come at you on the slant, or sideways. Flux is biggest when the field hits the surface square on; if it skims along the surface, the flux is nought, nothing's getting "through". The formula: Φ only counts the field part along the surface normal.

charge.b:
How big the point charge is, in nanocoulombs (10⁻⁹ C). Its field is E = kQ/r² with k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C².
ELI5: a charge is like a tap; the bigger the Q, the harder the field pours out. 5 nC is grand and safe, but 5 full coulombs? That's lightning territory, so it is.

chargepos.b:
Where the source charge sits, in metres. Mind now: don't stick it on (or inside) the surface, the 1/r² field goes absolutely bananas, and the Monte Carlo result's not worth a clock.
ELI5: keep the electric balloon up in the air, not glued to the middle of the sheet.

customfield.b:
Free-form vector field: E = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ as functions of (x,y,z), in N/C. Say: ⟨−y, x, 0⟩ spins around; ⟨0, 0, 1⟩ blows upward; a charge at (0,0,2) gives ⟨k(x−x₀), k(y−y₀), k(z−z₀)⟩/r³, build it yourself.
ELI5: this is the pro desk: make the field any shape you like, once it's in N/C you're laughing.

flip.b:
Flux carries a sign depending on how the surface is facing. Normal +z means out the "top".
ELI5: it's like choosing to face the window in or out: rain coming in is +, going out is −. The total Φ flips sign, but "how much" field pokes through stays the same altogether.

mc.b:
Instead of a symbolic integral (pure torment for a wavy surface), we hurl N random points across the domain, work out each one's flux bit g = −P·fₓ − Q·f_y + R, then average the lot: Φ ≈ (Domain area)·mean(g).
ELI5: want to know how much rain lands in an oddly shaped garden? scatter N buckets around the place, measure them, take the average. Easy.

samples.b:
How many random points. The error drops ~1/√N: 100× more points only buys you 10× less error.
ELI5: more dice rolls, closer to the truth. 100,000 rolls usually lands you within ~0.3%; want it tighter again? crank up N.

seed.b:
The starting number for the random engine. Same seed, same result, exactly the same.
ELI5: like a film with a rewind button: the experiment can be repeated scientifically. Leave it blank if you want a fresh result every run, sure.

ai.b:
You write a scenario in plain words → it goes to an LLM (OpenRouter, the key's in config.json) → the AI hands back a JSON config (surface, field, domain, flux direction) → the backend checks the formulas and numbers mathematically (the AI can't sneak in code, don't be worrying) → parameters fill the form → the Python module runs the Monte Carlo.
ELI5: the AI is only a clever typing assistant; the physics calculator on the backend does the actual sums.

matrix.hint: Bain úsáid as roghchlár na réimse (Insert matrix) le haghaidh maitrís NxN ar bith, agus líon na cealla le huimhreacha.

ode.hint: Use y' and y'' for derivatives. Example: y'' + y = sin(x)

hydro.use3: P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^{2} + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^{2} + \rho g h_2

poly.hint: Cuir isteach an polynóim iomlán p(x) thuas, m.s. x^2 - 5x + 6, agus roghnaigh fréamhacha nó fachtóiriú. Déantar oibreán cosúil leis an tsuimiúchin comhtháite a mheas ar dtús go huathoibríoch.

gr.hint: Leave r empty to compute the radius only. r must be bigger than the Schwarzschild radius.

heatexp.use3: Q = m\,L \;\text{(phase change without temperature rise)}

gsurf3d.use2: \text{tangent plane: } z = f_0 + f_x\Delta x + f_y\Delta y

gdist.use1: P(a \le X \le b) = \text{area under the PDF}

sims.lg_hint: Logistic map x(k+1) = r·x(k)(1−x(k)). Raise r slowly: fixed point → period 2 → 4 → chaos.
sims.lz_hint: Lorenz system via RK4. Defaults σ=10, ρ=28, β=8/3 = the classic butterfly attractor.
sims.fo_hint: f is evaluated numerically on [−L, L] (N max 60). Try f(x)=x, |x|, or x².
sims.mx_hint: Fill the 2×2 matrix cells. Plot: unit circle → ellipse, unit square → parallelogram, arrows = basis e₁,e₂ and their images.
sims.w_hint: Random unit steps (uniform angle), the seed fixes the outcome, same seed, same result.
sims.dp_hint: RK4 Δt = 0.002 s. Energy is conserved (drift ~1e-7%). Large angles = chaos: try θ₁ = 170°.
sims.dr_hint: RK4 with quadratic drag F = ½ρCₑAv². Dashed curve = vacuum. Defaults = a baseball.
sims.ke_hint: μ = GM (free units). Starts at perihelion with vis-viva speed. Compare the measured period with Kepler's Third Law.
sims.sl_hint: On-screen intensity: I = cos²(πdy/λL) × sinc²(πay/λL). a = 0 → ideal double slit.
sims.qm_hint: Natural units ħ = m = 1. A Gaussian packet hits a square barrier; split-step Fourier integration.

sslit.use1: I(y) = \cos^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{\pi d y}{\lambda L}\right) \cdot \mathrm{sinc}^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{\pi a y}{\lambda L}\right)
